cells.tense: You are walking it at the pace the ground actually shows you.
cells.ask: Put one thing you've been picturing into a concrete next step today, and notice whether that step feels level or tilted. What you feel there is the correction.
cells.core:
The light you have is enough for the next step and you're not pretending it's more. You've been through enough that your imagining is tied to ground — what you picture tends to have something underneath it, and people probably notice that.

What keeps it steady is remembering the half-road you can't see isn't a failure of the light; it's the condition. When the picture stays connected to the next real move, your vision recalibrates the room around you instead of running off with it. The balance asks something of you: it will keep feeding the drive to go only as long as you keep checking the ground under each picture.
cells.sheetLine: Enough light for the next step, and you walk it.

cells.tense: You will be living in a version that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Name what rests on the picture being real, then do one small thing that only requires today to be true. Let the picture hold if it can.
cells.core:
The picturing has gone past the next step. You're living in a version that hasn't happened, and getting there is the point — so the picture starts standing in for the thing. What's ahead gets treated as already settled, and the people and facts in front of you get adjusted to fit it instead of the other way.

That's where the balance tilts. You've stopped handling what's real at today's size, and the gap between the picture and the ground is doing quiet damage you won't feel until it's big. The piece that corrects it isn't dreaming smaller. It's feeding what's actually in front of you, and letting that tell you what's real.
cells.sheetLine: The picture has started standing in for the thing.

cells.tense: You stand at the door of the symbolic and you've stopped opening it.
cells.ask: Say one image out loud — to yourself or someone — and stay with it for a minute without explaining it away. Notice where your attention goes.
cells.core:
You know what matters before you can say why, and you've been treating that as noise rather than signal. You stopped leaning on your own sense of things and started only trusting what could be measured or argued. None of that is where you are now; it's just the shape of how you stand.

What's missing is comfort with not knowing — the kind where a perception just lands. And the way in is indirect: you don't push yourself to feel more. You start by paying attention to what already draws you, one thing at a time, and letting it prove itself at its own pace.

cells.tense: You are already picturing a life, and you talk as if it were just how things are.
cells.ask: Pick one routine you do and finish it with attention. Let the practice be small and repeatable. What it connects you to is yours to find.
cells.core:
You're already shaping a life with pictures you're not owning as yours. The imagining happens — in what you reach for, what you allow, what you keep circling — and you describe it as just the situation or just your personality. At its best, that picturing stays tied to something you've actually lived through, and the picture grows out of what's already in your hands instead of pulling you off the ground.

What's missing here is owning it. The fix isn't a big decision. It's picking one small, repeatable practice and giving it your attention — the kind that connects you to something rather than isolates you in it. What you find there is yours, and you're free to name it so.
cells.sheetLine: You picture a life already. Nobody's told you it's yours.

attempts.check: The draft I'm warned against would claim this person's dreaming is already steering their life — the record says only that the capacity to move without full clarity is present and can be claimed, not that any particular course is being steered. A reader could say 'no, I'm not dreaming anything and I don't feel steered,' and the reading still has to leave them something to use. The ask survives being wrong because it's one act in the open, not a verdict on their history. The sentence that serves me more than them is the poster line about trusting the road; it's cut.
